title: A Stormy Thanksgiving Across America
summary:
Thanksgiving was very different this year for millions of people in America. Big storms swept across the country on Thursday, bringing floods, strong winds, and power cuts that changed holiday plans from coast to coast.

By Thursday evening, more than 900,000 customers in at least eight states had lost power. Two storm systems stretched from Maine to Florida, and strong winds hit the West Coast.

In Ocean City, Maryland, gusts of up to 65 miles per hour tore the roof off a building. Near Washington, D.C., a tree fell on a house where people were inside, but officials said no one was hurt.

Flood water almost covered downtown Stone Harbor, New Jersey. New Jersey and New York both declared states of emergency.

Meteorologist Matthew Cappucci of MyRadar.com warned that more people could lose power. He said a fast river of wind high in the sky, moving at about 80 miles per hour, was feeding the storms.

Some places had snow for Thanksgiving instead. Travel was hard: FlightAware counted more than 1,900 flight delays and over 400 cancellations.
why_it_matters: Storms like these can change your own holiday plans, knock out the power at home, and delay trips to visit family.

keywords.explanation: A gust is a sudden, strong rush of wind.
A meteorologist is a person who studies the weather and predicts storms.
A state of emergency is when leaders say a place needs extra help and special rules because of danger.
A cancellation is when a planned flight or event is called off and does not happen.
A storm system is a large area of bad weather that moves across the country.

background_read: Thanksgiving is a big holiday in America when families get together to share a meal and give thanks.
A storm is a spell of wild weather, with strong winds, heavy rain, or snow, that can knock down trees and power lines.
When a storm is very strong, leaders can declare a state of emergency, which means extra help and special rules are put in place to keep people safe.
